meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: India – Size and Location
meta.intro: India’s geographical location, latitudinal and longitudinal extent, size, neighbours and strategic position in the Indian Ocean.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s major geographical concepts and processes.
Identify important locations and features on an outline map of India.
Relate physical geography to people, resources, environment and development.

blocks.text: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere. Its mainland extends from 8°4′N to 37°6′N and from 68°7′E to 97°25′E. These coordinates help identify the country’s position on a globe and explain its broad climatic setting.

The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N) passes almost through the middle of India. It divides the country into broad tropical and subtropical zones, although altitude, relief and monsoon winds also shape regional climates.
The southernmost point of the Indian Union is Indira Point in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The mainland’s southern tip is Kanyakumari. These are different locations and should not be confused.
India has an area of about 3.28 million square kilometres, approximately 2.4 per cent of the world’s geographical area. It is the seventh-largest country in the world by area.
The north–south extent is about 3,214 km and the east–west extent about 2,933 km. The longitudinal extent creates a time difference of nearly two hours between the eastern and western ends.
India’s coastline, including island groups, is about 7,516.6 km. Its long coastline supports ports, fisheries, coastal settlements and maritime trade.
The local time difference between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh is nearly two hours because the Sun appears to move across longitudes at different times.
To maintain one uniform time for the entire country, India uses 82°30′E as its Standard Meridian. It passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Indian Standard Time is UTC+5:30.
A single standard time makes railway schedules, administration, broadcasting, communication and national coordination easier.

India occupies a central position at the head of the Indian Ocean. The Deccan Peninsula projects southwards into the ocean, placing India near major sea routes between Europe, Africa, West Asia and East and Southeast Asia.
The western coast provides access towards the Arabian Sea, Persian Gulf and eastern coast of Africa. The eastern coast faces the Bay of Bengal and routes towards Southeast Asia.
The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 shortened the sea distance between India and Europe, increasing the importance of maritime trade routes.

India shares land boundaries with Pakistan and Afghanistan in the northwest; China, Nepal and Bhutan in the north; and Bangladesh and Myanmar in the east. Sri Lanka and the Maldives are maritime neighbours.
Sri Lanka is separated from India by the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar. The Maldives lies to the southwest of Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea.
Map practice: mark the Tropic of Cancer, Standard Meridian, Kanyakumari, Indira Point, neighbouring countries, Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.
